question: Does the discrete-time Jacobian of SGD make negative-curvature directions locally expansive, and do Hessian-spectrum pruning and finite-time perturbation experiments show that such expansion is both necessary for effective neural-network training and responsible for persistent trajectory divergence?

key_findings.claim: The paper uses 'chaos' in a deliberately restricted sense: sensitivity to initial conditions, not the standard three-part definition of a chaotic dynamical system.
key_findings.evidence: Section 2.1 states that formal chaos also requires topological transitivity and dense periodic points, and its footnote adds that a rigorous definition requires a bounded invariant set. The study then explicitly uses 'chaotic' only for sensitivity to initial conditions because that property is considered relevant to optimization. The title and conclusion should therefore be read as claims about local or finite-time trajectory expansion, not a demonstration of full chaos in SGD.

key_findings.claim: For deterministic one-step SGD dynamics with a fixed sampled batch, negative Hessian eigenvalues are locally expansive, while sufficiently large positive eigenvalues are expansive as well.
key_findings.evidence: Writing the update Jacobian as I minus learning-rate times Hessian gives a local Lyapunov exponent of log absolute-value of one minus learning-rate times the Hessian eigenvalue. Thus every negative eigenvalue produces a multiplier above one, and a positive eigenvalue also does so when it exceeds the two-over-learning-rate threshold. This is a clean discrete-time curvature result, but the derivation explicitly discounts random batch sampling and establishes a local linear expansion criterion rather than global chaos.

key_findings.claim: The claimed theorem that Chaos-sensitive Gradient Descent guarantees non-exponentially-diverging orbits omits the parameter dependence of the spectral projector and therefore does not establish the advertised guarantee for the implemented adaptive map.
key_findings.evidence: CGD recomputes a projector from current Hessian or local-Lyapunov eigenvectors and applies it to the gradient. In the official supplemental proof of Theorem A.7, differentiation of the update retains the Hessian derivative of the gradient but treats the projector v(theta)v(theta)^T as constant; the derivative of this eigenspace projector is absent. Unless the projector is externally frozen, that missing product-rule term changes the Jacobian. The main theorem consequently supports an instantaneous frozen-projector intervention, not a general guarantee for a state-dependent CGD trajectory.

key_findings.claim: Removing the full negative or locally expansive eigenspectrum slows or stalls training in the tested small networks, whereas removing the positive spectrum has a smaller early effect.
key_findings.evidence: The experiments compute and diagonalize the full Hessian at every step for a 784-20-10 MLP and a small two-dimensional CNN on USPS and downsampled FashionMNIST. In the main USPS plots, negative-spectrum and full-chaotic pruning sharply reduce learning speed and attained accuracy, including when pruning begins after 2k, 5k, or 10k steps. Positive-spectrum pruning initially reaches much stronger performance. The official supplement reproduces the qualitative negative-pruning slowdown across the second dataset, architectures, activations, and momentum choices.

key_findings.claim: The pruning experiment does not isolate sensitivity to initial conditions as the causal resource; it directly removes descent components in negative-curvature directions that are already expected to help leave saddles.
key_findings.evidence: CGD projects the gradient away from selected Hessian eigenspaces, changing its direction and generally its norm. The authors' own explanation is that negative curvature marks directions with future loss-improvement potential and that removing those components prevents exploration. Without matched-norm random-subspace, sign-preserving, or trajectory-expansion-only controls, poorer optimization after projection shows that the removed curvature directions matter, but not that exponential sensitivity itself is necessary.

key_findings.claim: The paper's own extended results weaken the claim that the positive Hessian spectrum is less important.
key_findings.evidence: The main text emphasizes that positive-spectrum pruning has only a small performance effect over the displayed window. In the official supplement, however, full positive-spectrum pruning repeatedly makes loss singular and crashes MLP and CNN runs on USPS and FashionMNIST; with momentum it drives the non-chaotic eigenvalue count to zero. Conversely, some negative-pruned FashionMNIST runs eventually approach comparable training performance, albeit more slowly. The robust conclusion is a time-dependent optimization tradeoff, not a general ranking that positive curvature is dispensable.

anchors.section: Three empirical conclusions about Hessian spectra

key_findings.claim: Finite-time Lyapunov spectra in the tested runs move from early expansion toward exponents near zero, but this does not establish asymptotic edge-chaos.
key_findings.evidence: The authors multiply time-varying tangent maps, diagonalize the resulting finite-time Lyapunov matrix, and report maximum exponents above zero early in training that approach zero later. The main text then labels the limiting regime edge-chaotic. Yet the measured quantities are finite-horizon estimates on short small-model runs, the minimum exponent is numerically unstable in the supplement, and no asymptotic limit, invariant set, or statistical uncertainty is established. Near-zero finite-time exponents are compatible with slow drift, flat symmetries, numerical error, or nonstationary training as well as genuine edge-chaos.

key_findings.claim: The headline ordering of perturbation directions is fragile and was selected at one admitted cherry-picked perturbation magnitude.
key_findings.evidence: The main paper presents epsilon=0.1 because its distances follow the expected order and says larger perturbations violate locality while smaller ones appear dominated by probable numerical noise. Official supplemental Section C.4 is more direct: epsilon=0.1 'can be said to be cherry picked,' both smaller and larger magnitudes become increasingly random, and the cause of the fixed-seed noise is unknown. At epsilon=0.1, the supplement reports no significant accuracy difference across perturbation strategies. The experiment therefore illustrates one local geometry slice rather than a robust direction-specific causal effect.

key_findings.claim: The random-walk-plus-linear divergence law is a descriptive finite-window fit, not a validated mechanism for late-training SGD trajectories.
key_findings.evidence: The proposed distance curve assumes a deterministic component whose cumulative norm grows linearly plus independent isotropic Gaussian noise, yielding the square root of a quadratic and linear term. It is fitted to observed USPS curves, but the paper does not test held-out horizons, compare alternative diffusion laws, establish Gaussian or independent noise, or derive the constant drift from SGD. The authors acknowledge that they could not run long enough to see whether distances saturate and that the model may fail at longer times.

key_findings.claim: Persistent parameter divergence is not shown to harm predictions or generalization in these experiments.
key_findings.evidence: Perturbed models continue moving apart in Euclidean parameter distance after training accuracy plateaus, but the main study focuses mainly on training metrics and does not measure function-space disagreement, calibration, robustness, or generalization gaps caused by the divergence. The supplement reports no significant accuracy differences among epsilon=0.1 perturbation strategies. Parameter symmetries and flat minimum manifolds can support large weight-space distances with nearly identical functions, so the operational consequence remains unresolved.

anchors.section: 5 Discussion: training-metric scope and future generalization work

key_findings.claim: Exact full-spectrum computation restricts the evidence to tiny architectures and prevents the paper from validating its intrinsic-chaos claim in modern training regimes.
key_findings.evidence: Every pruning step requires the full Hessian and eigendecomposition. The experiments therefore use only a one-hidden-layer MLP and a very small CNN, batch size eight in the released configuration, USPS, and 16-by-16 FashionMNIST. The paper explicitly says it cannot extend to higher-dimensional data or models and does not test batch normalization, residual connections, transformers, adaptive optimizers, or realistic large-scale schedules. Hessian-vector products may estimate only the top divergence bound, but they do not make the full CGD intervention scalable.

method.core_idea: Treat SGD as a discrete dynamical system, derive its tangent map from the Hessian, suppress locally expansive eigendirections to test their necessity, and use finite-time Lyapunov perturbations to characterize long-run trajectory separation.
method.mechanism: For SGD without momentum, the local tangent multiplier is I minus learning-rate times Hessian. The paper defines local Lyapunov exponents from that Jacobian, labels negative-curvature and over-threshold positive-curvature directions locally expansive, and constructs CGD by projecting each gradient onto the complement of selected Hessian eigenspaces. Separately, it accumulates tangent maps to obtain finite-time Lyapunov eigenspaces, perturbs a converged model along maximal, random, and non-expansive directions, and fits pairwise parameter distance with a deterministic linear-drift plus Gaussian-random-walk model.
assumptions: Sensitivity to initial conditions is an adequate operational proxy for chaos even without topological transitivity, dense periodic points, or a demonstrated bounded invariant set.
The minibatch sequence is fixed or synchronized, so random batch sampling can be discounted when differentiating the SGD map.
A first-order tangent approximation is accurate for the chosen perturbation magnitude and observed horizon.
Hessian and local-Lyapunov eigenvectors are sufficiently well defined despite degeneracies, near-zero eigenvalues, and non-smooth ReLU networks.
The state-dependent spectral projector may be treated as locally fixed when claiming CGD's non-expansion guarantee.
Removing a curvature subspace is a valid intervention on chaos rather than a confounded intervention on descent direction and update magnitude.
The small MLP and CNN on USPS and downsampled FashionMNIST represent broader neural-network optimization behavior.
Near-zero finite-time Lyapunov exponents forecast an asymptotic edge-chaotic regime.
Euclidean parameter distance is meaningful despite permutation, scaling, and flat-manifold symmetries.
Late distance can be decomposed into constant linear drift and independent isotropic Gaussian noise over the measured window.

techniques.role: Links one-step trajectory expansion to the Hessian through the Jacobian I minus learning-rate times Hessian.
Classifies current Hessian eigendirections as locally expansive or contractive.
Projects gradients away from all or selected locally expansive eigenspaces.
Starts the CGD intervention later to test whether the slowdown is restricted to initialization.
Supplies exact small-model curvature spectra and projectors at every training step.
Accumulates tangent maps to estimate expanding and contracting subspaces over a training interval.
Compares maximal, random-subspace, and fully random perturbations of the same trained initialization.
Checks whether late expanding and non-expanding subspaces remain similar enough to reuse for perturbations.
Provides a compact descriptive model for continuing parameter separation after performance plateaus.

evaluations.setting: A 784-20-10 MLP with ReLU or sigmoid activation on USPS, with and without momentum.
evaluations.metric: Training and validation accuracy/loss after pruning full chaotic, negative, or positive Hessian spectra.
evaluations.result: Negative and chaotic pruning substantially slow learning; positive pruning reaches high performance sooner but several supplemental runs later become singular.
evaluations.baseline: Standard SGD from the same initialization and positive-versus-negative spectrum pruning.

evaluations.setting: A small two-dimensional CNN on USPS and 16-by-16 FashionMNIST.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy/loss trajectories under the same spectral interventions.
evaluations.result: Negative and chaotic pruning again delay or suppress learning in the displayed horizon, while positive pruning can initially learn quickly and then crash.
evaluations.baseline: Unmodified SGD and the other spectral-pruning choices.

evaluations.setting: Delayed CGD activation after 2,000, 5,000, or 10,000 steps in a sigmoid MLP.
evaluations.metric: Change in loss and accuracy slope immediately after pruning begins.
evaluations.result: Optimization slows at each intervention point, showing that the removed directions remain useful beyond the earliest phase.
evaluations.baseline: The uninterrupted SGD trajectory before and without intervention.

evaluations.setting: Finite-time Lyapunov tracking across MLP/CNN, USPS/FashionMNIST, and momentum/no-momentum configurations.
evaluations.metric: Maximum and minimum finite-time exponents and dimensions of expanding/non-expanding subspaces.
evaluations.result: Maximum exponents start positive and approach zero; the paper interprets this as a transition from chaotic to edge-chaotic dynamics.
evaluations.baseline: Comparison over training time and across model/optimizer configurations rather than a separate estimator.

evaluations.setting: Five perturbation directions derived from the final finite-time Lyapunov eigenspace, primarily at norm 0.1.
evaluations.metric: Euclidean distance from the unperturbed parameter trajectory and final moving-average accuracy.
evaluations.result: Distances continue growing after accuracy plateaus and show the intended directional ordering at norm 0.1, but the supplement calls that norm cherry-picked, reports increasingly random ordering elsewhere, and finds no significant accuracy difference at 0.1.
evaluations.baseline: A completely random perturbation plus maximal/random expansive and maximal/random non-expansive directions.

evaluations.setting: Late-trajectory parameter separation on USPS and FashionMNIST.
evaluations.metric: Fit of distance versus update count to the square root of a quadratic drift term plus a linear diffusion term.
evaluations.result: The two-term curve matches the observed finite window, but saturation, mechanism identification, and out-of-window prediction are not tested.
evaluations.baseline: Visual fit to observed distances and Lyapunov-derived first-order upper/lower bounds.

limitations: The paper operationalizes only sensitivity to initial conditions, so its use of 'chaos' is narrower than the standard dynamical-systems definition.
The local theory conditions on a deterministic or synchronized batch sequence and does not characterize stochastic random dynamical systems under independent minibatch draws.
The non-expansion proof omits derivatives of the state-dependent Hessian-eigenspace projector.
Projection removes useful gradient components and changes update norms, confounding causal claims about trajectory sensitivity.
Only small MLPs and CNNs, two simple image datasets, and short horizons are tractable with exact full Hessians.
The study omits batch normalization, residual networks, transformers, Adam-family optimizers, realistic schedules, and large datasets.
Most plotted interventions appear to use one shared initialization and provide no seed-level uncertainty or statistical tests in the main paper.
Positive-spectrum pruning eventually crashes in several supplemental experiments despite being described as less consequential in the main text.
Finite-time exponents approaching zero do not prove the infinite-time limit or an edge-chaotic invariant regime.
The perturbation-direction ordering is robust only at an admitted cherry-picked magnitude of 0.1.
Numerical noise dominates smaller perturbations despite fixed random seeds, and its source remains unresolved.
Euclidean weight distance does not account for functional equivalence, symmetries, or flat solution manifolds.
The drift-plus-random-walk model assumes constant deterministic separation and isotropic independent Gaussian noise without testing those assumptions.
The training horizon is too short to determine whether trajectory distances saturate.
No demonstrated predictive, generalization, calibration, or robustness consequence follows from the measured parameter divergence.
failure_modes: Near-degenerate Hessian eigenvalues can rotate projectors abruptly, invalidating smooth tangent and fixed-subspace approximations.
A positive Hessian eigenvalue above the two-over-learning-rate threshold can itself be expansive, so negative-only pruning does not guarantee local stability.
Removing every negative-curvature component can trap optimization near saddles even if trajectory sensitivity was not harmful.
Removing the positive spectrum can leave only expansive negative-curvature updates and produce the singular losses seen in the supplement.
ReLU non-differentiability and finite numerical precision can destabilize Hessians, matrix logarithms, and eigenvector orderings.
Independent minibatch sequences create trajectory separation from exogenous noise that the deterministic tangent map does not distinguish from sensitive dependence.
Parameter rescaling and permutation symmetries can create large Euclidean distances without meaningful functional divergence.
Finite-time exponents close to zero can be misclassified because numerical error accumulates in long Jacobian products.
A perturbation larger than the local linear neighborhood invalidates Lyapunov-vector predictions; a smaller one can fall below numerical noise.
Fitting both drift and diffusion terms on one horizon can mimic many nonstationary separation curves and extrapolate incorrectly.
Full Hessian eigendecomposition is cubic in parameter dimension and becomes unusable before modern model scale.
reusable_insights: Separate local one-step expansion, finite-time sensitivity, asymptotic Lyapunov exponents, and formal chaos instead of using one label for all four.
When intervening on an eigenspace, include the derivative of the state-dependent projector or explicitly freeze it and narrow the theorem.
Use matched-norm random-subspace and norm-restored controls to separate the value of negative-curvature information from the value of instability itself.
Track function-space disagreement, calibration, and validation behavior alongside weight-space distances.
Sweep perturbation magnitude on a preregistered logarithmic grid and report the full locality-versus-numerical-noise phase diagram.
Estimate Lyapunov quantities with QR reorthogonalization and report precision, condition numbers, degeneracy handling, and uncertainty.
Compare synchronized and independently sampled minibatch streams to distinguish deterministic sensitivity from stochastic forcing.
Use symmetry-aware or mode-connectivity distances before interpreting parameter separation as different learned solutions.
Validate late-time drift models by fitting early windows and predicting held-out horizons, with alternative diffusion exponents and saturation models.
Replace full spectra with Hessian-vector products only after defining a low-rank intervention whose causal estimand remains clear.
Report both transient optimization benefits and eventual instability when positive and negative curvature have stage-dependent roles.
open_questions: Does a correct Jacobian including eigenspace-projector derivatives preserve any non-expansion guarantee for adaptive CGD?
Can trajectory expansion be altered without removing negative-curvature descent information, enabling a clean causal test of chaos?
How do Lyapunov spectra change when perturbed runs receive independent rather than synchronized minibatches?
Do the early-positive and late-near-zero finite-time exponents persist in ResNets, transformers, batch-normalized models, and AdamW training?
Which function-space quantities, if any, continue to diverge after parameter distance grows?
Is the late regime diffusive, ballistic, anomalously diffusive, bounded, or a mixture after much longer training?
Can symmetry quotienting or minimum-loss-manifold coordinates explain the apparent linear drift more parsimoniously?
Are negative-curvature directions valuable because they enable saddle escape, feature discovery, discrete-time instability, or some separable combination?
Can scalable stochastic Lanczos or Jacobian-vector estimators recover stable Lyapunov subspaces with calibrated errors?
What learning-rate, batch-size, and momentum phase diagram separates negative-curvature expansion from positive-curvature edge-of-stability oscillation?
Do chaotic transients improve time-to-accuracy or generalization under compute-matched modern baselines, as later work proposes?
Can the cherry-picked perturbation result be independently reproduced across seeds, precisions, libraries, and eigensolvers?

competitive_landscape.title: A Chaos Theory Approach to Understand Neural Network Optimization
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest direct predecessor connecting SGD Lyapunov exponents to negative Hessian curvature.
competitive_landscape.difference: Sasdelli et al. use a continuous-time approximation and estimate the maximum exponent on larger CIFAR-10 models; Herrmann et al. emphasize discrete-time multipliers, the full spectrum, and causal projection interventions on much smaller networks.
competitive_landscape.source_version: DICTA 2021 author paper and official DOI record

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational empirical account of discrete gradient dynamics beyond the positive-curvature stability threshold.
competitive_landscape.difference: Cohen et al. find top positive Hessian eigenvalues hovering near two over the step size in practical full-batch training; the reviewed paper's small-step experiments find almost no positive locally expansive modes and attribute expansion mainly to negative curvature.

competitive_landscape.title: Self-Stabilization: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.relationship: Competing nonlinear explanation for locally unstable discrete gradient dynamics.
competitive_landscape.difference: Damian et al. show that cubic structure can bound and self-stabilize top-eigenvector oscillations and explicitly argue the edge-of-stability regime is not necessarily chaotic; this challenges inference from a locally expansive linearization to sustained chaos.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding the Unstable Convergence of Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporary theory and experiments on convergence despite violation of local smoothness stability conditions.
competitive_landscape.difference: Ahn et al. characterize non-monotone but convergent dynamics beyond two over sharpness without requiring full Lyapunov spectra; their results reinforce that local linear instability does not by itself imply globally chaotic optimization.

competitive_landscape.title: Negative eigenvalues of the Hessian in deep neural networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct curvature predecessor on the optimization value of negative Hessian directions.
competitive_landscape.difference: Alain et al. study whether optimizers exploit negative curvature; their framing supplies a non-chaos explanation for why projecting those directions out can hurt, which the reviewed intervention does not control away.

competitive_landscape.title: Escaping Saddles with Stochastic Gradients
competitive_landscape.relationship: Competing mechanism for the utility of SGD components along negative-curvature directions.
competitive_landscape.difference: Daneshmand et al. prove that stochastic-gradient variance aligns with negative curvature and enables saddle escape; this predicts damage from negative-subspace pruning without asserting that sensitive dependence itself is beneficial.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Network Weights Do Not Converge to Stationary Points: An Invariant Measure Perspective
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest contemporary alternative explanation for continuing weight motion after loss stabilizes.
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. demonstrate non-convergence on ImageNet ResNet101 and WikiText Transformer-XL and model convergence in distribution to an approximate invariant measure; Herrmann et al. use small-model pairwise distances and a fitted drift-plus-random-walk law.

competitive_landscape.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent-Induced Drift of Representation in a Two-Layer Neural Network
competitive_landscape.relationship: Adjacent theory of persistent drift with stable task behavior.
competitive_landscape.difference: Pashakhanloo and Koulakov decompose motion into bounded normal fluctuations and diffusion tangent to a minimum-loss manifold, giving a geometric mechanism that the reviewed isotropic random-walk fit does not model.

competitive_landscape.title: The Implicit Regularization of Dynamical Stability in Stochastic Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.relationship: Competing stability-centered account of SGD's Hessian-dependent implicit bias and generalization.
competitive_landscape.difference: Wu and Su derive stability constraints involving Hessian trace or Frobenius norm and prove generalization consequences for structured models; the reviewed work instead argues that local expansion is unavoidable and offers no generalization theorem for its measured divergence.

competitive_landscape.title: Leveraging chaos in the training of artificial neural networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct later work testing whether transient positive Lyapunov exponents can accelerate training.
competitive_landscape.difference: Jimenez-Gonzalez et al. sweep unusually large learning rates across broader architectures and tasks and find minimum time-to-accuracy near the onset of positive maximum exponents; it tests a constructive hyperparameter prediction rather than pruning curvature directions.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v1 and 2026 Physical Review Research record

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Descent with Large Step Sizes: Chaos and Fractal Convergence Region
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later rigorous study of sensitivity and fractal convergence boundaries under large-step gradient descent.
competitive_landscape.difference: Liang and Montufar derive an exact critical step size and fractal initialization boundary in matrix factorization, providing explicit long-run outcome sensitivity; the reviewed paper studies finite-time expansion and unresolved distance growth in generic small classifiers.

competitive_landscape.title: Riddled basin geometry sets fundamental limits to predictability and reproducibility in deep learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later work connecting chaotic learning dynamics to outcome-level unpredictability through basin geometry.
competitive_landscape.difference: Ly and Gong analyze riddled basins and uncertainty exponents, directly testing whether arbitrarily close initializations reach different outcomes; the reviewed paper measures growing parameter distance while accuracy remains similar.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Stability of Nonlinear Dynamics in GD and SGD: Beyond Quadratic Potentials
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current theory examining when linearized instability faithfully predicts nonlinear GD and SGD behavior.
competitive_landscape.difference: Mulayoff and Stich show that nonlinear dynamics may stably oscillate around a linearly unstable minimum, directly limiting conclusions drawn from the reviewed paper's Hessian-based local expansion test.

competitive_landscape.title: SGD at the Edge of Stability: The Stochastic Sharpness Gap
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current stochastic extension of edge-of-stability dynamics.
competitive_landscape.difference: Liao et al. derive how projected minibatch noise shifts the equilibrium top curvature below two over the step size and prove a stochastic coupling theorem; this is a more explicit treatment of batch noise than the reviewed fixed-batch tangent analysis.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first time-discrete full-spectrum link from neural-network curvature to chaotic SGD dynamics, introduces a spectrum-pruning optimizer that guarantees non-chaotic updates, and shows that negative-curvature chaos is intrinsic to successful training while late trajectories remain edge-chaotic.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The discrete one-step criterion, exact full-spectrum intervention, delayed-pruning experiment, and finite-time perturbation toolkit are concrete contributions beyond the closest 2021 continuous-time chaos analysis. However, edge-of-stability, negative-curvature saddle escape, non-convergent weights, and Lyapunov analyses all predate or closely flank it. The non-chaos guarantee omits projector derivatives; pruning confounds instability with useful descent directions; the main spectral ranking is softened by supplemental crashes; and the global perturbation result depends on an admitted cherry-picked magnitude.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The durable novelty is a small-scale diagnostic case study connecting discrete Hessian multipliers, spectral interventions, and finite-time trajectory geometry. It does not establish that formal chaos is universal or causally necessary for modern SGD. A compelling successor would use correct state-dependent Jacobians, matched causal controls, synchronized-versus-independent batch streams, symmetry-aware function distances, preregistered perturbation sweeps, and scalable estimates on modern architectures.

reviewer_notes: Read the exact 11-page official NeurIPS 2022 proceedings PDF end to end. Because the main paper delegates nearly all proofs and extended experiments to a separate artifact, I also downloaded and read the official 27-page appendix from the proceedings supplemental ZIP (ZIP SHA-256 af12a847c289fc8cbcd1b943d6cca7fc007eedde8c34852f86a0311ad0bf6e39; appendix PDF SHA-256 27f99ab688c8e58577775dcdc692234efb4caea0b39c4ec308ce56b9b303e1cc), and inspected the released README and experiment configurations. The pinned reading provenance remains the indexed 11-page paper, so all formal page anchors stay within it; supplemental section names are stated in evidence where material. The strongest audits are the missing derivative of the parameter-dependent spectral projector in Theorem A.7, the explicit C.4 admission that epsilon=0.1 was cherry picked, the unresolved numerical noise at smaller perturbations, the absence of accuracy effects at epsilon=0.1, and eventual singular loss under positive-spectrum pruning. Fourteen competitors were checked against primary arXiv, OpenReview, or official proceedings records through 2026-08-23. An independent mathematical reviewer should verify the projector-derivative objection, the momentum tangent-map formulas, matrix-log edge cases, and all code-to-paper settings before verified promotion.
